passage: The four girls in Room 12 of the working women's hostel had a problem: the bathroom. Payal cleaned it every Sunday; the others forgot. By the third week, she was furious. She left a sticky note: "I'm not your maid." Madhuri, the youngest, took it personally and cried. That evening the warden suggested they sit together. Payal took a breath and said, "I'm sorry about the note. I'm tired of doing it alone." Madhuri said she hadn't known it was a problem because nobody said anything. They made a rota on the fridge, split the cost of cleaning supplies, and agreed to raise things at a weekly ten-minute check-in. It wasn't perfect, but Payal stopped seething on Sundays.

qa.q: What did Payal write on the sticky note?
qa.a: She wrote, "I'm not your maid."

qa.q: Why did Madhuri cry after reading the note?
qa.a: She took it personally and felt accused, especially since nobody had told her there was a problem.

qa.q: What made the roommates' final solution fair?
qa.a: They talked openly, split chores with a rota, shared supply costs and set up weekly check-ins to raise issues early.

qa.q: How might the warden see the girls' solution?
qa.a: She might be pleased they resolved it themselves with a clear system instead of letting the conflict grow.

grounding: It shows young women in a hostel resolving a chore conflict by talking and sharing work and costs fairly.

passage:
Hi Hafsa,
I'm writing this instead of talking because I get flustered, and I want to say it right.
I've noticed the electricity bill is much higher since the heater came in. I also know you work night shifts, so it's needed. But I'm paying half and I'm hardly home. Could we split it based on use, maybe 60-40, or you cover the heater months?
Also, the kitchen. I know I left dishes last week, and I'm sorry. Can we both wash our own on the same day?
I really like living with you. I don't want small things to become big things.
Tell me what you think; I'm open.
Karthik

qa.q: What split of the bill did Karthik suggest?
qa.a: Karthik suggested 60-40, or that Hafsa cover the heater months.

qa.q: Why did Karthik choose to write instead of talking?
qa.a: Karthik gets flustered in person and wanted to express the concerns carefully and fairly.

qa.q: What made Karthik's note fair?
qa.a: Karthik acknowledged Hafsa's needs, owned the mistake with the dishes, offered options and stayed open to Hafsa's view.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel reading this note?
qa.a: Hafsa might feel a little defensive about the bill, but likely appreciate the respectful tone and Karthik's apology.

grounding: A young adult's note to a flatmate negotiates shared bills and chores fairly.

passage: You want to know how we stopped fighting? I'm Chandrika. Rashmi and I share a two-bedroom flat in Chennai, and for the first three months it was a war. She played music at midnight. I left my laundry on the chair for days. We both paid rent late, and our landlord shouted at both of us. One night she said, "I'm about to move out." That scared me. So we sat on the floor with snacks and wrote down what drove us crazy. It was honestly funny. Hers: my laundry. Mine: her music. We agreed on quiet hours after 11, a laundry deadline, and a shared account for rent. Now we fight maybe once a month, about who ate the last mango.

qa.q: What time did they agree quiet hours would start?
qa.a: Quiet hours would start after 11.

qa.q: Why was Chandrika scared when Rashmi said she might move out?
qa.a: She realised their fights were serious enough to end the arrangement, and she didn't want to lose her flatmate.

qa.q: What made their floor-and-snacks talk work?
qa.a: They named specific problems honestly, kept it light, and agreed clear rules for noise, laundry and rent.

qa.q: How might the landlord see them now?
qa.a: The landlord likely has fewer complaints, since their shared account means rent is paid on time.

grounding: A young woman describes how she and her flatmate managed conflict fairly over noise, chores and money.

passage: I share the flat in Andheri with Ritu and Zubin, so I had a front-row seat. The electricity bill had jumped, and Ritu kept glancing at Zubin's gaming setup, which ran most nights. For a week she said nothing and just stacked his unwashed pans pointedly by the sink. I couldn't tell if she was angry or just tired. Then on Sunday she put the bill on the table and asked if we could sit for ten minutes. She didn't accuse him. She suggested splitting the base amount equally and Zubin paying a bit extra for the months he games a lot. Zubin looked defensive at first, arms crossed, then shrugged. 'Fair. Can we also do a dishes chart? I'm bad at noticing.' The chart is still on the fridge, slightly crooked.

qa.q: In which area is the flat the narrator shares with Ritu and Zubin?
qa.a: In Andheri.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling during the week she stayed silent?
qa.a: The narrator could not be sure, but stacking the pans pointedly suggests frustration building up that she had not yet put into words.

qa.q: Why did Sunday's conversation work better than the silent pans?
qa.a: Ritu chose a calm time, used the bill as a shared fact and proposed a fair split instead of blaming, so Zubin could agree and add his own idea.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt when Ritu put the bill on the table?
qa.a: Defensive at first, as his crossed arms show, but her calm offer let him admit he is bad at noticing and help fix it.

grounding: A flatmate observes roommates settling a money and chores conflict fairly after a tense week.

passage: Day 1: Salma found her milk finished again and a note in Kiran's handwriting: 'Sorry! Will replace.' It was the fourth note that month. She typed a long angry message, deleted it, and left for college, jaw tight all day. Day 4: Over chai in their PG kitchen in Kochi, Salma said, 'I like living with you, but the borrowing is costing me money and patience.' Kiran went red. 'I thought the notes made it okay.' They agreed on a shared jar for milk, bread and oil, each putting in the same amount every Monday, with personal things on separate shelves. Day 20: The jar ran low, and Kiran topped it up without being asked, adding a packet of Salma's favourite biscuits. Salma laughed and stuck a note on it: 'Forgiven, twice over.'

qa.q: Which items did the shared jar cover?
qa.a: Milk, bread and oil, with each of them putting in the same amount every Monday.

qa.q: Why did Salma delete her long angry message?
qa.a: She was upset but seemed not to want a written fight to damage a friendship she valued, so she waited to talk calmly in person.

qa.q: What made their agreement fair?
qa.a: Shared basics were paid for equally and personal things stayed on separate shelves, so neither had to track small debts or feel taken for granted.

qa.q: How did Kiran see the borrowing before Day 4?
qa.a: Kiran genuinely thought the 'Sorry! Will replace' notes made it okay and did not realise what it was costing Salma.

grounding: Shows roommates moving from silent resentment to a fair shared-money system over three weeks.

passage: Irawati, you think four girls in one flat is hard? Let your Rajni Masi tell you about Room 14. We were three in a hostel room built for two, in Lucknow, 1998. Sushma kept her lamp on till two, Jaya left dishes under the bed, and I, madam, used everybody's soap. For a month we sulked and stuck notes on the mirror. Then one night Jaya's dishes grew a smell even I couldn't ignore, and I shouted. Jaya cried. And Sushma, the quiet one, said, "Let's each say one thing that bothers us and one thing we'll change. No shouting." So we did. Lamp off at midnight. Dishes washed by morning. Soap, my own. And we pooled for a kettle, everybody the same share. It wasn't perfect. But Jaya is still my dearest friend. Sit, I'll tell you what she said about my soap.

qa.q: What was Jaya's habit that caused trouble?
qa.a: Leaving dishes under the bed.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when Rajni shouted?
qa.a: Jaya felt hurt and upset and cried, after a month of tension burst out as shouting.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Room 14, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sushma's rule of one complaint and one change each, with no shouting, turned blame into fair, specific agreements everyone could keep.

qa.q: How might Sushma have seen the month of sulking and mirror notes?
qa.a: Sushma, the quiet one, probably felt tired and uneasy with the tension, which may be why she proposed a calmer way to talk.

grounding: An aunt tells how three hostel roommates turned sulking into fair agreements about chores, space and shared costs.

passage: The electricity bill arrived in the hottest week of May: nearly double. Kalyani stuck it to the fridge with a mango magnet and waited. Deepak, who worked from home and ran the cooler in his room all day, saw it first and went quiet. Hema, the third flatmate, was away at her sister's. Kalyani had rehearsed an angry speech in the shower. Instead, at dinner, she said, "The bill doubled. I'm not blaming anyone, but splitting it three ways doesn't feel fair when we use it so differently." Deepak rubbed his neck. "It's the cooler. I can't work in forty-two degrees." "I get that," she said. "Can we note the meter every evening for a week and agree a fairer split once Hema's back?" He thought, then nodded. They messaged Hema together straight away, so she wouldn't come home to a deal already made.

qa.q: How much had the electricity bill gone up?
qa.a: It had nearly doubled.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he saw the bill and went quiet?
qa.a: Deepak likely felt guilty and a bit defensive, knowing the cooler he ran all day was probably the cause.

qa.q: What made Kalyani's approach at dinner fair?
qa.a: She named the problem without blaming, accepted Deepak's need to work in the heat, and suggested measuring before deciding.

qa.q: What would change for Hema if the others had decided without her?
qa.a: Hema would come back to a deal made without her voice and might feel left out or resentful, even if the split was fair.

grounding: In a heatwave, flatmates negotiate a fair way to share a doubled bill, including the absent flatmate.

passage: By the third week in their Andheri flat, the bathroom had become a silent war. Ritu cleaned it on Sundays. Vishal said he would "do it next time", and next time never came. Rather than write another sarcastic note, Ritu waited until he was making his evening omelette. "Can we talk chores for five minutes?" He flipped the omelette, wary. "Is this about the bathroom?" "Partly. I've done it four Sundays. I'm starting to resent you, and I don't want to." Vishal winced. "I hate cleaning it. I'd rather do the grocery runs, the gas bookings and the dishes every night." Ritu considered. Dishes every night was more work than one bathroom a week. "Deal, if the dishes really happen. Check in next Sunday?" They wrote it on a sheet taped inside a kitchen cupboard, where guests wouldn't see.

qa.q: How many Sundays had Ritu cleaned the bathroom?
qa.a: Four Sundays.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling before raising the chores?
qa.a: Ritu was starting to feel resentful about doing the bathroom alone, and worried that the resentment would sour things between them.

qa.q: Why is a check-in next Sunday a good part of the deal?
qa.a: It gives both a chance to see whether the swap is working and adjust fairly before resentment builds again.

qa.q: How does Vishal see the chore swap?
qa.a: Vishal is relieved to trade the task he hates for ones he'd rather do, and his wince suggests he knows he had been unfair.

grounding: Two flatmates in Mumbai turn a silent chore conflict into a fair trade with a check-in.

passage:
"Afreen, we need to talk about the kitchen," said Ayesha, holding a burnt pan.
"I know, I know. I was going to wash it."
"That was two days ago."
Afreen sighed. "Okay. Fair. But you leave lights on all night, and the electricity bill is split equally."
Ayesha blinked. "…That's also fair."
"So what do we do?"
"A chart. Dishes the same day, whoever cooks. Lights off when you leave a room. And we split the bill by using the meter photos each month."
"And if one of us breaks the rule?"
"Buy the other one samosas."
Afreen laughed. "Deal."
They stuck the chart on the fridge. The next day, Afreen washed the pan without being asked.

qa.q: What was Ayesha holding?
qa.a: A burnt pan.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling while saying "That was two days ago"?
qa.a: Ayesha felt frustrated and annoyed about the unwashed pan.

qa.q: What made the negotiation work?
qa.a: Both admitted their own habits, then agreed on clear rules and a light-hearted consequence.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the chart?
qa.a: Afreen sees it as fair, which is why Afreen washes the pan the next day without being asked.

grounding: Two young flatmates negotiate chores and bill-sharing fairly.

passage:
In my second year, I shared a flat with Gopika and two others. For months, I was the one doing all the dishes. I didn't say anything. I just got angrier, banging pots loudly.
One night Gopika asked, "Why are you so grumpy?" And I exploded. "Because I'm the only one who ever cleans!"
She looked stunned. "Why didn't you say?"
I realised I'd expected them to read my mind.
We sat down that weekend and made a rota. Gopika took dishes on weekdays; I took the bathroom. We shared groceries through a notebook.
I'm Anirban. I learnt that silent resentment makes conflict worse. Saying it early, calmly, would have saved us months.

qa.q: What did Gopika take on weekdays after the rota?
qa.a: Dishes.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling while banging pots?
qa.a: Anirban felt resentful and angry about doing all the dishes.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Anirban's position?
qa.a: Raise it early and calmly, instead of expecting flatmates to read your mind.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt when Anirban exploded?
qa.a: Gopika was stunned and probably a bit hurt, since she hadn't known there was a problem.

grounding: A young adult reflects on silent resentment in a shared flat and learning to negotiate.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, women's block.
Mehak and Parul, roommates in Room 12, came to me separately this week. Mehak said Parul plays music late and has friends over at midnight. Parul said Mehak switches off the lights at ten and complains about everything.
Today I met them together. I asked each to say what she needs most. Mehak: sleep before exams. Parul: some social time.
They agreed: music with headphones after ten, friends leave by eleven, and on weekends Parul can host later if Mehak isn't there.
Parul offered to help Mehak with the fan that squeaks, which Mehak had also complained about. They laughed.
I'll check in after two weeks. — Mrs Das

qa.q: Which room are Mehak and Parul in?
qa.a: Room 12.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she complained to the warden?
qa.a: Mehak felt frustrated and tired, worried about sleep before exams.

qa.q: What did Mrs Das do that helped resolve the conflict?
qa.a: She met them together, asked each what they needed most, and helped them agree on clear compromises.

qa.q: How might Parul feel about the agreement?
qa.a: Parul likely feels heard, since her need for social time was respected too.

grounding: A warden helps two young roommates resolve conflict fairly.

passage:
Monday
Pranav's diary. The flat is at war over dishes. Lavanya cooks every night, which is great, but she leaves every pot for "later", and later is apparently next week. I've been washing them, and getting quietly furious.
Also the electricity bill came. Lavanya's heater runs all night. She suggested we split it equally. I said nothing and felt like a doormat.
Tonight I finally said, "Can we sit down for ten minutes?" I was nervous. I said the dishes were bothering me, and asked if we could split the bill based on who uses the heater, or take turns on who pays extra in winter.
She actually said, "Oh god, sorry, I didn't notice." We made a chart: whoever cooks doesn't wash. And she'll pay a bit more of the winter bills.
I should've spoken up two weeks ago.

qa.q: What did Lavanya and Pranav decide about cooking and washing?
qa.a: Whoever cooks doesn't wash.

qa.q: How had Pranav been feeling before the talk?
qa.a: Pranav had been quietly furious about the dishes and felt like a doormat about the bill.

qa.q: What made the flat meeting work, and what could Pranav do differently next time?
qa.a: Pranav asked calmly for ten minutes and suggested fair options; next time Pranav could speak up early instead of waiting two weeks.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt hearing Pranav's concerns?
qa.a: Lavanya seems surprised and a bit embarrassed, as she genuinely hadn't noticed, and was willing to fix it.

grounding: Illustrates flatmates negotiating chores and a shared bill fairly after one of them speaks up.

passage:
Deepak and Tanuja had both got teaching posts in the same small town in Odisha and rented a two-room house near the market to save costs. Two months in, it was tense.
Deepak left his clothes everywhere. Tanuja took phone calls with her family till midnight, and the walls were thin. Neither said anything, but they had stopped eating together.
Then the landlord's wife said, loudly, "You two fight like a married couple without talking." Tanuja laughed, and something cracked open.
That night they sat on the back step. Deepak admitted the calls kept him awake. Tanuja admitted the clothes made her feel like a maid. They agreed: calls on the back step after 10, clothes in his room, and a shared cleaning morning on Sundays.
It wasn't perfect. But they started eating dinner together again, and on Sundays they argued about music instead.

qa.q: Where did Deepak and Tanuja agree calls would happen after 10?
qa.a: On the back step.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel about Deepak's clothes lying around?
qa.a: Tanuja felt resentful, as if she were being treated like a maid.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: They avoided talking and stopped eating together; honestly naming each problem and agreeing on specific rules fixed it.

qa.q: How might the landlord's wife see the two of them after that night?
qa.a: She might notice they seem friendlier, eating together and arguing only about music.

grounding: Illustrates housemates in a small town moving from silent tension to fair negotiation over shared space.

passage: The sink in the Manchester flat had been full for four days when Bilal finally taped a note to the kettle: "Can we talk tonight? Not angry. Just tired of the dishes 🙏" Emeka read it and came in with two mugs of tea. "Sorry, man. My shifts at the warehouse changed. I'm barely home." Bilal had rehearsed a speech about fairness all afternoon, but it softened. They sat at the wobbly table and listed every chore on the back of the electricity bill. Emeka took the bins and the bathroom, which he could do on his late mornings; Bilal took the dishes on weekdays. For the heating, they agreed to split the bill evenly and set the thermostat somewhere both could live with. Emeka stuck the list on the fridge. "Review in two weeks?" "Deal."

qa.q: Where did Bilal tape his note?
qa.a: He taped the note to the kettle.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling before the talk, and how did it change?
qa.a: He was frustrated and tired of the dishes, rehearsing a speech about fairness, but softened into understanding once Emeka explained the changed shifts.

qa.q: What made their negotiation fair?
qa.a: They listed every chore together, matched tasks to each person's schedule, and agreed to review the plan in two weeks.

qa.q: How does Emeka see the pile of dishes?
qa.a: Emeka feels sorry and a bit embarrassed, and sees it as a result of the new warehouse shifts rather than not caring.

grounding: Shows two roommates sharing chores and a bill through a calm, fair negotiation.
